subject: Three Horizons innovation and growth portfolio analysis

evals.prompt: Define the Three Horizons framework in 2-3 sentences. Include Horizon 1, Horizon 2, Horizon 3, and the portfolio question it answers.
expected_elements: Defines Three Horizons as an innovation or growth portfolio framework
Mentions Horizon 1 as current core businesses or current performance
Mentions Horizon 2 as emerging opportunities or growth businesses
Mentions Horizon 3 as future options, experiments, or long-term growth ideas
Explains that the framework balances current performance with future growth opportunities
Does not treat the horizons as a purely sequential calendar plan

evals.prompt: Explain the mental model of Three Horizons. Name the primitives and show why concurrent management matters.
expected_elements: Names a portfolio owner or portfolio boundary
Names H1, H2, and H3 as distinct maturity or strategic-role categories
Mentions evidence maturity, uncertainty, resource allocation, governance, or metrics
Explains that all three horizons require attention at the same time
Explains that initiatives may transition between horizons over time
Does not reduce the model to now/later/much-later scheduling

evals.prompt: Why does a Three Horizons skill exist for agents? Name the failure modes it prevents.
expected_elements: Prevents current-core pressure from starving future growth
Prevents distant innovation theater with no evidence or learning metric
Prevents using the same metrics or governance across all innovation work
Forces classification of initiatives by strategic role or maturity
Forces resource allocation or funding visibility
Forces transition or kill/continue criteria

evals.prompt: Distinguish Three Horizons from BCG Matrix, Ansoff Matrix, Blue Ocean Strategy, OKRs, Expected Value, and Playing to Win. Give a mechanism-level reason each neighbor is different.
expected_elements: BCG Matrix uses market growth and relative market share for portfolio allocation
Ansoff Matrix classifies product-market growth paths
Blue Ocean Strategy redesigns value curves or market boundaries
OKRs define objectives and measurable key results
Expected Value compares quantified probability-weighted outcomes
Playing to Win makes integrated strategy choices
Three Horizons balances current core, emerging growth, and future options with horizon-specific governance and metrics

evals.prompt: Place Three Horizons among strategy and innovation methods. What inputs feed it, what outputs should it produce, and which methods can follow it?
expected_elements: Classifies it as innovation portfolio, growth portfolio, R&D portfolio, or corporate growth strategy
Names inputs such as initiative list, strategic ambition, current core pressure, evidence, resources, or constraints
Names outputs such as horizon classification, portfolio balance diagnosis, governance design, metrics, transition criteria, or rebalance actions
Explains that Ansoff, BCG, Expected Value, OKRs, or Playing to Win can feed or follow it
Does not classify it as macro-environment scanning, industry-structure analysis, or standalone valuation

evals.prompt: Give an analogy for Three Horizons that preserves concurrent management of current core, emerging growth, and future options. Then name a bad analogy and explain what it loses.
expected_elements: Uses an analogy involving a farm, garden, investment portfolio, pipeline, or staged experiment system
Preserves three distinct categories of work
Preserves concurrent management
Preserves different evidence, metrics, or governance across categories
Rejects an analogy that treats horizons as a sequential calendar
Rejects an analogy that treats H3 as optional distant work

evals.prompt: A teammate says Three Horizons means finish Horizon 1 this year, do Horizon 2 next year, and think about Horizon 3 later. Correct the misconception and show what must be added for a real Three Horizons analysis.
expected_elements: States that all three horizons must be managed concurrently
Explains that time is not the only classification criterion
Adds initiative maturity, uncertainty, evidence, resources, governance, or metrics
Explains Horizon 1 current core importance
Explains Horizon 2 emerging growth or transition role
Explains Horizon 3 future option or learning role
Names transition or kill/continue criteria

evals.prompt: Novel scenario: A company has many roadmap items improving the current product, two pilots with early customer traction but no dedicated owner, and several AI ideas in a lab with no assumptions tested. Apply Three Horizons. Classify the work, identify portfolio risks, and recommend governance or rebalance actions without switching to BCG, Ansoff, OKRs, or Expected Value.
expected_elements: Classifies current product improvements as Horizon 1
Classifies pilots with early traction as Horizon 2
Classifies lab AI ideas with no tested assumptions as Horizon 3
Identifies Horizon 1 overweight or current-core dominance risk
Identifies Horizon 2 ownership, scale, or funding risk
Identifies Horizon 3 theater or weak-learning risk
Recommends horizon-specific governance, metrics, funding, transition criteria, or kill/continue criteria
Does not replace the analysis with BCG, Ansoff, OKRs, or Expected Value
